[← Previous post: *Exorcising a Demon III: From Bristol to Bristol*](../exorcising-a-demon-bristol-to-bristol/){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

Before explaining just how wrong I was about my final-year project, I need to
take a detour. Rereading the first three parts of this series, I noticed that I
had moved from paranoid defeatism to cautious optimism without losing the habit
of making jokes at my own expense. The little bit of Britain I had acquired
thought, good grief, this sounds like a soap opera. A restrained Englishman
might have said that university had been “a bit difficult” and left it there.

Perhaps there is some melodrama in them, but the Filipino heart was doing most
of the talking. My family, friends and lecturers were not supporting characters
in an individual story; they were part of how I understood myself. Perhaps it
was only then that I began to see the people at Bristol as *kapwa*, rather than
as potential judges.

## Filipino Nurses and a Tennis Player

That is why this detour begins in an NHS hospital ward. Most of us will need a
nurse eventually, and Britain has a horde of Filipino nurses. One of them may
well be caring for you. Their care may feel unusually personal: more patient
than the circumstances reasonably permit or more concerned about your comfort
than the job strictly requires.

This is not a theorem about Filipino nurses. A population of more than a hundred
million people will provide counterexamples to almost any proposition. I am
interested in the narrower question of why some Filipino nurses appear to treat
care as something more personal than a professional transaction.

To understand that, consider Alex Eala. Her ranking bears her name, and she wins
or loses her own matches. Yet Filipinos [fill courts wherever she
plays](https://www.rolandgarros.com/en-us/article/alex-eala-janice-tjen-top-50-2026-season-fans-asia-progress-clay-courts).
They queued for hours at Wimbledon and followed her to Washington, where she
won her [first tour-level WTA
title](https://www.wtatennis.com/tournaments/1045/washington-dc/2026/past-winners).
The Philippines, which is not known as a tennis country, promptly developed
several million experts on second serves.

After her Wimbledon run, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr [received her at
Malacañan Palace](https://pco.gov.ph/news_releases/president-marcos-hails-alex-eala-as-ph-tennis-champion-vows-full-government-support/)
and praised the way she carried her Filipino identity onto the court. Eala has
said much the same thing herself: [where she comes from forms part of who she
is](https://www.wtatennis.com/news/4530020/alexandra-eala-history-first-filipina-third-round-grand-slam-the-philippines-in-wimbledon-it-means-so-much).
She competes on an individual professional tour, yet Filipinos experience her
victories as partly theirs.

## The Audience in My Head

I understand this because something similar happened inside my head at
Bristol. There was no flag beside my name on an examination paper, but I worried
that my performance reflected upon Filipinos generally. If I struggled, I felt
that I was confirming somebody’s doubts about us; if I did well, I felt that I
had defended a national reputation nobody had asked me to defend.

My lecturers had imposed none of this. They could distinguish one Filipino with
a chequered academic history from an entire country. If I failed Linear Algebra,
nobody was going to summon the Philippine ambassador. The audience was largely
imaginary, but that did not make it harmless.

[Virgilio Enriquez’s concept of
*kapwa*](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1360870767498462848) helps explain it. Enriquez,
the founder of *Sikolohiyang Pilipino*, argued that Filipino psychology should
begin with Filipino language and experience rather than assume that concepts
developed elsewhere would fit us perfectly.

*Kapwa* is sometimes translated as “other person”, although that loses much of
its meaning. In English, the other is separate from me. With *kapwa*, the other
person and I share something of the same identity. This does not mean Filipinos
live in perpetual harmony; anyone who has attended a Filipino family gathering
will know better. It means that the boundary between what belongs to me and what
belongs to others is not always absolute. For better or worse, *kapwa* forms
part of our cultural firmware.

I had encountered this when I left content creation. I had around two million
followers, most of whom were Filipino, and many felt betrayed when I left public
life to return to university. They did not want me to remain stupid; they had
simply come to regard my political work as something we shared, so my departure
did not appear to be an entirely private decision.

Looking back, I suspect they understood my departure through *kapwa*. I was
trying to finish the education I had abandoned; they saw me walking away from
something in which they had also invested. I cannot blame them, but leaving was
something I had to do. The work bore my name without belonging only to me.

## Back to the Ward

The same idea may help us understand your Filipino NHS nurse. I am not a nurse,
and using [retinal images in a mathematics
project](https://github.com/reyjosephnieto/ph) does not qualify me to speak for
one. I suspect, however, that *kapwa* explains part of what patients sometimes
experience as unusually personal care.

A patient may begin as a stranger but remains *kapwa*: another person whose
suffering is not entirely separate from one’s own. There is also
*pakikiramdam*, the effort to notice what another person feels without waiting
for a formal request. The nurse is unlikely to think, “I shall now demonstrate
Filipino culture to Bed 12.” They may simply find it difficult to walk away
while somebody remains frightened or uncomfortable.

Professional training, experience and temperament still matter. *Kapwa* is not
a complete explanation, but it helps explain why care may feel personal even
when the relationship began as a professional one.

There is also a danger. Describing Filipinos as naturally caring, selfless and
hardworking gives an overstretched health service a convenient excuse for
expecting too much from them. A [study of Filipino nurses in
Britain](https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/35114/) noted that, during the
first two months of the COVID-19 pandemic, Filipinos were estimated to account
for 36 per cent of known healthcare-worker deaths despite comprising about 8
per cent of the NHS nursing workforce. Being good at caring for other people
does not make somebody indestructible.

Eala should be allowed to lose without feeling that she has failed the
Philippines. I should have been able to perform badly in an examination without
treating it as an international incident. A Filipino nurse should be able to
finish a shift without believing that exhaustion represents a failure to care.

*Kapwa* is not the demon that needs exorcising. It fills tennis courts for a
young woman from Quezon City, helped the son of a pig farmer and grandson of a
rice farmer survive at a university half a planet away, and can make a
frightened patient feel that somebody sees them. The demon is the belief that
belonging must always be earned through achievement and sacrifice.

If a Filipino nurse cares for you, say thank you, but do not mistake that
kindness for an unlimited resource. *Kapwa* may help explain why they care; it
does not mean they do not need caring for. As for my final-year project, that
particular disaster will have to wait.
